metadata.title: Claude, Deal Team Summary.
metadata.subtitle: The Deal-Team-Summary Skill
metadata.purpose: Teardown-register conversion of the deal-team-summary reel: take apart what an Anthropic skill actually is (a folder + a plain-language SKILL.md read before Claude acts), explain the mechanism (linear steps, no branching), and judge the design choice — they optimized for repeatable structure at the expense of judgment. Facts unchanged from source: the five-field shape (parties, key terms, status, open issues, next steps), the Aster Corp / Vale Robotics illustrative deal, and the note that structure isn't a fact-check.

beats.narration_text: The natural read is that Claude just writes a deal team summary — reads the docs, produces the summary, done. That's not what's happening. It's opening a folder, reading a file of instructions, and doing exactly what the file says. The file is called a skill. Let's take one apart.

props.text:
Claude writes a deal
team summary by
magic?

beats.narration_text: Here's the situation the skill exists to fix. A merger is in flight. The lawyers, the bankers, and the executives all need the same picture — parties, key terms, status, open issues, next steps. Five fields, one shared shape. Ask five people to write that update and you get five different shapes for the same deal. The information is stable; the container isn't. That's the problem.

items.label: Parties, terms, status, issues, next steps
items.sub: A merger needs one shared picture: parties, key terms, status, open issues, next steps.

items.label: Ask five people, get five shapes
items.sub: Ask five people for that update, and you get five different shapes for the same deal.

beats.narration_text: The natural assumption is that Claude already knows how to shape this. It's read enough deal documents in training — good judgment should be enough, no separate instructions required. Here's why that assumption breaks: judgment isn't a shape. A model that has read every M&A memo ever written can still produce two different memos for the same deal, on the same day.

items.label: Claude already knows how to shape this
items.sub: The natural assumption: good judgment, no separate instructions required.

items.label: It's read plenty of deals
items.sub: It's read enough deal documents before to just handle it.

beats.narration_text: Here's the test that breaks the assumption. Ask for the same deal's summary twice, with no skill installed. Read the two answers side by side. Different fields. Different order. Sometimes an item drops out entirely. Neither answer is wrong — they're both reasonable readings. But they're not the same summary. Judgment isn't repeatable; that's the property a deal room needs.

items.label: Same deal, asked twice, no skill
items.sub: Ask for the same deal's summary twice, with no skill installed.

items.label: Different fields, different order, missing items
items.sub: The two answers don't match — different fields, different order, sometimes a missing item.

beats.narration_text: Here's what a skill actually is. A folder on disk. This one's called deal-team-summary. Inside it, one file — SKILL.md. Plain markdown, no hidden code, nothing compiled. Claude reads that file before it touches the deal documents. The file is the whole program. That's a design choice: instructions are text, not code, so the lawyer whose deal this is can open the file, argue with a step, and change it.

items.label: deal-team-summary: one file, SKILL.md
items.sub: A skill is a folder Claude reads before it acts — this one called deal-team-summary.

items.label: Plain language, no hidden logic
items.sub: Inside is one file, SKILL.md — plain language. The file is the instructions.

beats.narration_text: Inside SKILL.md is a numbered list of steps. Claude reads them top to bottom and runs each one — pull the parties, pull the terms, check status, flag open issues, list next steps. Linear. No shortcuts, no cleverness, no re-ordering to be more efficient. That's the point. The same steps in the same order, so the output shape is fixed by the file, not by whatever Claude happened to feel like on that pass.

items.label: Parties → terms → status → issues → next steps
items.sub: Claude reads the steps in SKILL.md and runs each one in order.

items.label: Linear. No shortcuts.
items.sub: No branching unless the file itself says so.

beats.narration_text: Take one illustrative deal — Aster Corp buying Vale Robotics. Hand the skill the term sheet, the disclosure schedule, and the latest redline. The output comes back with the same five fields: parties, terms, status, open issues, next steps. Not because Claude decided those were the right fields — because SKILL.md said so, before Claude ever opened the documents.

items.label: Term sheet, disclosure schedule, redline
items.sub: One illustrative deal: Aster Corp buying Vale Robotics. Feed the skill the source documents.

items.label: Same five fields, every time
items.sub: Parties, terms, status, open issues, next steps — the same shape comes back.

beats.narration_text: Now run it again a week later, after the redline changes. Same five fields, same order — only the contents update. That's what a skill actually buys: the shape holds while the deal moves. Two summaries a week apart, and someone who read the first one knows exactly where to look in the second. The container is stable; the payload isn't.

items.label: Same deal, one week later
items.sub: Run it again after the redline changes.

items.label: Same five fields, same order
items.sub: Only the contents update — the shape holds, the deal moves.

beats.narration_text: Here's what a consistent shape doesn't do. It doesn't prove the deal is healthy. The skill structures whatever the documents say — a clean clause, a bad clause, a stale draft nobody's noticed is stale. Structure isn't a fact-check. That's an honest trade: they optimized for repeatability, not for judgment. If you want the clauses evaluated on their merits, that's a different skill — or a human lawyer.

items.label: A consistent shape isn't a healthy deal
items.sub: The skill structures whatever the documents say — good or bad.

items.label: Including a bad clause or a stale draft
items.sub: Structure isn't a check on the underlying facts.

beats.narration_text: And the flip side: two summaries that look different without the skill aren't necessarily wrong. They can both be reasonable readings of the same documents, just organized in different orders. That's the exact inconsistency the skill removes — not by making Claude smarter, but by making the shape of the answer non-negotiable.

items.label: Two summaries, no skill, both look different
items.sub: They aren't necessarily wrong — just organized differently.

items.label: That's the inconsistency the skill removes
items.sub: Same input, same structure, every single run.

beats.narration_text: A skill doesn't make Claude better at judgment. It makes Claude follow the same steps, in the same order, every single time. That's the whole trade — you swap judgment for structure. Worth it exactly when the structure is what the deal team actually needs.

props.quote: A skill doesn't make Claude better at judgment. It makes Claude follow the same steps, in the same order, every single time.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I'm writing a summary of a live deal for the deal team. I have a term sheet and a signed NDA. Before you write anything, tell me the exact structure you'll use — the fields, and their order. Then write the summary. Then run it again from scratch, and tell me whether the structure changed. Go deeper: if the structure did change, is the second answer more thoughtful, or is the shape not yet stable enough to trust — and what would you change about the prompt to lock the shape?
